paragraphs: The scorched walls of the West Market had not all been pulled down when the skies over Chang’an finally cleared.

Beside a well in the rear courtyard of the Court of Justice stood a bamboo cot. Several black-clad clerks were putting cloths used in the autopsy into boiling water. Fu Rong had wrapped the black thread taken from the dead man’s wrist in a scrap of fine silk. It was almost invisible; only with sunlight shining through the silk did its stubborn dark line emerge.

The superintendent of the imperial weaving workshops arrived early, a wooden casket in his arms and ash from the dye house still on his cuffs. He asked Fu Rong for the thread. Rather than speak at once, he held it beneath his nose and picked apart one end with a fingernail.
“A carriage-curtain tassel,” he said. “Horsehair twisted into sheep’s wool, darkened with lacquer ash. It will survive years of wind and sand.”

He took two old samples from the casket and laid them in the sunlight. All three threads were much the same color, though their thickness varied. The one found on the horse dealer’s wrist was almost identical in weave to an old pattern kept by the military administration.
“Who has carriages like that in Chang’an?”

“Quite a few offices received them.” The superintendent opened an old ledger. “Central command, the Feathered Forest, the princely households. The accounts from the ninth year of Jianyuan are still here. Fu Chong’s residence received the most that year—eight lengths.”
The justice clerk sitting beside him immediately lifted his brush. Fu Rong laid his hand over the ledger.
“Write that his household received eight lengths. Do not write that the thread belonged to his household.”
The superintendent looked up, apparently relieved. “If a tassel breaks, you can take a piece from it and put it on another carriage. The thread tells you its method of weaving, not its owner.”

Fu Rong did not smile. On the table stood other sealed exhibits: the wolf-fang knife, an old badge from the imperial clan office, and a forged wooden pass recovered from the ashes of Pingkang Ward. Every object seemed to recognize the same master. None would bring him before the court.

That afternoon Fu Rong had the clerks move the records into an empty room. Two maps covered a long table: one traced the road between Chang’an and Ye, the other the capital’s wards, camps, and watermills. An old courier clerk grimaced when asked to count the carts that had passed the barriers in the preceding six months. “My lord, do you know how many donkey carts pass through Chang’an every day? No ledger could hold them all.”
“Start with caravans.”
“And their names?”
“They can change.”
“The cart plates can change too.”
“Carts still need roads. Men sleep at inns; horses eat fodder. Changing a plate won’t make an axle narrower overnight.”

After that no one could do anything but work. Files rose around their knees, the edges of the papers overlapping like the scales of dried fish. One new clerk could recognize characters quickly but was clumsy with his brush. On the third night he copied the place name Puban with the wrong character and was berated until his face turned red. Fu Rong took the faulty sheet and heard the old courier explain that the two spellings referred to different relay stations. He kept the original ledger on the desk instead of letting it be discarded.
On the seventh morning, the young clerk suddenly sprang up from the papers, striking his knee against the inkstone and tipping it over.
“I’ve found it.”

Everyone gathered around. Twelve days before the armory fire, a caravan carrying dye and leather had left Chang’an eastward with seven carts, six black and one dark red. The proprietor’s surname changed three times along the route. At Puban, the plates changed too. Only the number of carts and the distance between their wheels remained constant. Seven went to Ye; five came back. The ledgers said nothing about the other two. The dark-red cart ultimately returned to a carriage yard south of the city.
The owner of that yard was the horse dealer who had died in custody.
Fu Rong asked who had guaranteed the passage. The young clerk turned to the last page and went silent, pressing one finger to the entry.
Beside the vermilion seal were two characters: Fu Liang.

The household guard who had quietly left Fu Chong’s residence on the day of Wang Meng’s burial had also been Fu Liang. Fu Rong had pursued him as far as the old Xianyang road, where the rain had erased the wheel tracks. There he had vanished.
“Is he still in Beidi?”
“His wife and children moved there three months ago,” the clerk answered. “He owns no fields or shops in his own name. Even the carriage-yard lease was registered through another man.”

Fu Rong looked toward the window. In the old stockades of Beidi, a banner of the Fu clan had long carried more authority than documents from Chang’an. Now that the court was verifying service registers, three fortified settlements had barred the inspectors, claiming their winter grain was insufficient and asking to put the matter off until the spring equinox. Two officials sent with orders returned covered in dust, having never reached the granaries.

Fu Rong did not dispatch a great army. Twenty mounted officers of the Court of Justice rode north carrying a handwritten imperial order. They were to seek Fu Liang alone, not seize weapons from the settlements. The third stockade again denied knowing him. On the fourth evening, a Di captain came alone, leading his horse to the inspectors' lodging. He refused to step inside and kept winding the reins around his hand and undoing them.
“He’s at the mountain temple,” the captain said at last. “Someone is waiting there for him. If you don’t go tonight, they’ll leave by morning.”

The night wind rattled the tiles. The riders vaulted a low wall, broke through the temple doors, and found ashes spiraling over a brazier before the Buddha. Fu Liang crouched by the fire, his long sword still sheathed. One of his two attendants was pinned to the floor. The other fled over the back wall into a deserted ditch; his body was hauled from the icy water the next day.
All they saved from the brazier was half a booklet.

Its edges were charred, but the handwriting was fine and dense. Old unit, present assignment, home district, number of households that could be summoned: each entry had its place. Some names were circled in vermilion; others marked only “usable” or “observe.” The last pages were empty, the hemp binding exposed in the ashes like joints of a broken skeleton.
When Fu Liang was brought back to Chang’an, the locust tree outside Fu Chong’s residence was putting out its first pale green leaves.

In the prison, Fu Rong had the ropes removed from Fu Liang’s wrists and gave him a bowl of hot water. Fu Liang did not drink. He stared at a crack in the tabletop. Twenty years of campaigns had left the backs of his hands as coarse as bark. Half the nail of his left thumb was missing, crushed, it was said, beneath a horse’s hoof in a battle in Bingzhou.
“Who wrote this list?”
“I did.”
“Did Fu Chong order you?”
“My lord knows I served him for twenty years.”
“I asked who ordered you.”
Fu Liang looked up. “Nobody. I was afraid the court would inspect the rolls one day, and then no one would be able to find even the living men who once fought beside Lord Fu.”
“Why didn’t you surrender it to the Secretariat?”
“If I had, those men’s camps would have been broken up.”
“So you kept it for yourself.”
After a long silence, Fu Liang nodded.

Fu Rong unfolded the fragment of a letter. It did not contain the word rebellion. It instructed the stockades to guard their soldiers and protect their families, and to assemble under the old orders if the Xianbei moved first.
“Who would issue the old order?”
“Lord Fu.”
“Has he issued it?”
“Not yet.”
“Do you hope he will?”
Fu Liang’s face tightened in the lamplight. “I hope he never needs to.”

They turned to the seven carts. Fu Liang admitted having stood guarantor for leather goods from his master’s residence, but denied any part in the weapons sent into Ye. The shop had been recommended by Liu Cheng, an accountant in the household. Three days before Wang Meng’s death, Liu Cheng had returned home for a funeral; no family by that name existed in the Hedong village he listed as his birthplace. The man who had introduced Liu Cheng to the household, Zhou Ping, had once been a clerk in central command. His relatives and neighbors could not be found either.
“If you knew nothing of the cargo,” Fu Rong asked, “why did you go to Ye afterward?”
“To see Yueshou. The Yan men thought we meant to purge their old regiments. We feared they would raise the Yan banners behind our backs. I went to tell him: Lord Fu won’t move if you don’t.”
“Did Yueshou believe you?”
“Who would believe all of it?”
Fu Rong pushed the caravan records across the table. Fu Liang leafed through them with his damaged thumb. At the entry for Puban, his hand stopped.
“I arranged this relay station.”
“Yes.”
“But when I went to Ye I had four carts, carrying grain and cloth. This caravan had seven.”
“They used your route.”
“My inns, my stables, my men at the barriers.” Fu Liang stared at the vermilion mark. Sweat suddenly stood on his forehead. “Someone used my road. They didn’t even trouble to change my name.”
“Or you used it yourself.”

“Perhaps.” For the first time, fear entered his eyes. “You have enough to put me to death now, my lord. But I truly don’t know who sent weapons to Ye, or who arranged for that Xianbei soldier to die in the First Battalion.”

Fu Rong gathered up the records. Fu Liang’s proven guilt did not make him innocent of everything else; nor did the innocence he could not prove erase the evidence of another offense. As Fu Rong was leaving, Fu Liang called him back.
“If Lord Fu dies because of me, the old men of Beidi will rise.”
“Is that a threat?”
“I’m frightened,” Fu Liang said, eyes downcast. “I’ve followed him half my life. This is the first time I haven’t known whose orders to follow tomorrow morning.”
The next day Fu Chong was summoned to a side chamber of Chengming Hall.

He wore an old court robe with an inch of mending at one cuff, nearly invisible unless one looked closely. No attendants accompanied his carriage through the palace gate. His bodyguards were forbidden even to wait below the steps. The charred list, Fu Liang’s testimony, and a clan-office badge lay on the table. Fu Chong looked first at the list, then at the Heavenly King, and last at Fu Rong.
“The man is mine,” he said. “I told him to preserve the list as well. If Your Majesty has questions, ask me.”
“Did you order the stockades in Beidi to refuse their military registers?” Fu Jian asked.
“I told them to wait. Their old units are being broken up so quickly, and their land and families have not been settled. Who would surrender the last list of his comrades?”
“The new edict says amalgamation will not strip soldiers of their fields.”
“That is what Chang’an says.” Fu Chong glanced at Fu Hong. “Will the estate stewards in Beidi do as they’re told? If those men are driven from their military allotments, who will stand up for them?”

His words were not without force. Everyone in the hall knew that once a decree reached the provinces and passed through the hands of local clerks, it could acquire another face altogether. Fu Hong almost objected, then remembered the woman in Yanshou Ward asking who would acknowledge her wooden tally. He held his tongue.
Fu Jian leaned forward. “Even if there is graft, even if land is seized, you cannot circulate private military orders.”
“I did circulate them,” Fu Chong said. “Those stockade captains followed me into places where men did not return. If the Yan take up arms first, I will not tell them to wait at home for the sword.”
“You say 'if the Yan move first.' Who is to judge that?”
“I will judge the circumstances.”
“And if I command you to hold your men?”
“If the decree is truly yours, I will obey.”
Fu Hong spoke then. “What if someone says my father has been coerced by Murong Chui, and the decree is false?”
Fu Chong looked at him with the impatience of an elder toward a youth, but also with weariness. “Your Highness has never seen the gates of Chang’an opened by someone on the inside.”
“No, I have not,” Fu Hong said. “Then teach me, great-uncle: on such a day, should I trust the imperial decree or the general of my own house?”
Fu Chong opened his mouth but gave no answer.

Fu Jian ordered a senior justice officer to read the law aloud. Issuing private orders to garrisons and concealing service registers could, in grave cases, warrant exile. To convict a man of treason required further evidence: mustering troops, taking up arms against the sovereign, or openly disobeying command. No established evidence yet tied Fu Chong to the shipment of weapons to Ye, the murder in the camp, or the forged decree in Chang’an. There were plenty of men at court who would have liked to bind the three cases together and settle them under a single word—rebellion—saving themselves years of trouble.

Fu Jian regarded Fu Chong. As young men they had fought in the same ranks, once sharing half a bowl of hot gruel in the snow. Fu Chong’s eldest son had died in Bingzhou, his second in Hedong; Fu Jian had personally brought both notices of death to his house. Now the old general stood below him, his temples entirely white, still seeking to keep a blade in the hands of his kinsmen against whatever danger might come.
“Did you set the fire at Ye?”
“No.”
“Did you kill Helai Yan?”
“If I meant to kill a man, I would not resort to such a contemptible method.”
“And the forged decree?”
“I had nothing to do with it.”
“Contacting the Beidi garrisons and concealing their rolls?”
“I admit that.”
Fu Jian was silent for a long time. Beside the inkstone lay a spray of early peach blossom knocked down by rain overnight, its vermilion petals startling against the cold stone.
“Fu Chong, receive the sentence.”
The old general knelt.

Fu Jian stripped him of his title and military rank. His household contingents and military allotments were to return to official registration, though lawfully held private property would not be confiscated and his family would not share his punishment. Fu Chong himself was exiled to Shuofang, forbidden to communicate privately with his old regiments. Fu Liang was separately convicted of circulating military orders, hiding registers, and illicit contact; he was sent to a northwestern garrison and barred for life from military office. The investigations into the Ye incident, the camp murder, and the forged decree were to continue. No case file could be closed merely by invoking either man’s name.
Fu Chong heard the judgment with his forehead lowered. Then he asked hoarsely, “Your Majesty will spare my life?”
“I will.”
“And will you let me protest my innocence?”
“You will bear the penalty for what you have admitted. For what you deny, if the Court of Justice has no proof, I cannot confess it on your behalf.”
Fu Chong did not offer thanks. He remained bowed to the bricks for a long while. When he rose, his knees trembled slightly, but he held his back straight.
Three days later, they gathered at the western gate for his departure.

A great wind was blowing over Chang’an. Beyond the walls, dust dulled the first spring grass to gray. Fu Chong sat in an unlocked prison wagon, with four mounted justice officers escorting him front and rear. Hundreds of old soldiers had appeared outside the gate: one-eyed men, men with crutches, none wearing armor or carrying a blade. Someone had brought a jar of wine and set it on a stone by the road, yellow clay still clinging to the seal.
A young commandant had orders to disperse them. Seeing them stand quietly, he hesitated with his hand on his sword. Fu Rong came down from the city wall and told him to step aside.

As the wagon reached the wine jar, Fu Chong lifted its curtain. One by one the old soldiers pressed their fists to their breasts, offering the salute of the army that had founded the kingdom. No one called his official title, as though to speak it might make an old battle standard rise again from the dust.
Fu Chong signaled for the wagon to stop and saw Fu Jian standing above on the wall. Fu Jian came down. They met beside an earthen wall sheltered from the wind, with no one else near them.
“That list,” Fu Chong asked, “will Your Majesty burn it?”
“No. Soldiers must have names. Men who have left service must have homes to go back to.”
“Many on that list hate you.”
“I know.”
“You’ve taken the tally and sent me into exile. Do you think they’ll forget their old regiments?”
“No.”

Fu Chong touched his chest. The tiger tally was long gone. Wind lifted the empty strap where it had hung. He sighed. “All my life I led brothers into battle. I brought few of them home alive. Now I’ve handed over their names too. It feels as if I’ve abandoned the dead all over again.”
“Before your two sons went to war,” Fu Jian said, “you asked me to protect them. I failed. Today you ask me to protect these old soldiers as well.”
Fu Chong slowly raised his head.
“Then protect them for me.” His voice was hoarse. “If someone takes their land in Beidi, don’t make them walk a thousand li to Chang’an and kneel at your palace gate.”
Fu Jian promised.

Fu Chong went on. “I did not send the armor to Ye. Someone knows exactly what every household fears, and strikes where the fear is greatest. Yao Chang spoke to me too. He said that once the new army dismantled the old troops, an old man ought to leave himself some road of retreat.”
“Was that all he said?”
“That was all.”
“Do you suspect him?”
“I’ve suspected many people, Your Majesty. I’ve even suspected you.” Fu Chong gave a bitter smile. “That’s why I’m here.”
Fu Jian watched him. This old general had once been a loyal blade, straight and true. Now its edge was still turned outward, but might cut the hand that held it.

Fu Chong made a final bow as a subject and returned to the wagon. The old soldiers along the road held their salute until the whip sounded softly, the wheels passed the shadow of the wine jar, and the old man’s figure disappeared. A few shoulders shook. Most men simply stood there. No one followed the wagon.
Back at the palace, Fu Jian opened the box containing Wang Meng’s papers alone.

Much of the paper had yellowed. Each general at court had his own densely written note: service in the past, character, acquaintances. Fu Chong’s entry read: Deeply mindful of old debts, fiercely protective of former troops. Fit for command on campaign; not for prolonged independent rule over one district. Fu Jian took up his brush and added at the bottom: “Title removed; exiled to Shuofang.”
He turned the page. Yao Chang.

Wang Meng’s judgment described an outwardly deferential man with a guarded heart, still in constant touch with old Qiang associates. He should never hold the palace guard for too long, and certainly should not be given sole command over the Qiang again. Fu Jian’s brush halted beside the name. What Fu Chong had said was no evidence of a crime. The perfectly timed words of reassurance offered at Right Guard headquarters did not appear in any case file. One stroke of the brush—“arrest”—would help many men sleep that night. Asked the next morning to explain why, he would have only four words: “The Heavenly King suspects him.”
At last he laid down the brush.

Fu Rong arrived carrying a newly drawn map of the post roads. The Ye caravan, the forged passes used by Sun Fu, and the paper goods used for the Chang’an decree had all passed through an old document shop serving central command. The shopkeeper had drowned on the night Wang Meng died. His neighbors said he was drunk. He had long since been buried.
“Exhume him and examine the body again,” Fu Jian said.

Fu Rong saw the half-charred list left by Fu Liang on the table, and then Wang Meng’s unfinished register of names. “Elder brother, this book says who might still obey an old command; that one says whom the state should beware. The more we investigate, the more names we find.”

Fu Jian made no reply. He drew the two manuscripts together into the lamplight. One man had tried to find people within the old armies whom he could summon. The other had tried to preserve for the state the names of men it ought not to trust lightly. Half a lifetime’s care had been entrusted to a few faint lines of ink. Yet the man who killed Helai Yan was dead, the one who paid for the murder still unknown; the fire would say nothing, and the forged decree could not recognize the hand that wrote it.
“How did Feng Du die?” he asked.
“Not yet established.”
“Who originally held clan-office pass B-Twenty-One?”
“Still unidentified.”
“Who drove the lead wagon carrying armor to Ye?”
“Not established.”
Fu Jian pushed back the file. “Then write exactly that. Don’t be ashamed of the blank spaces.”

The palace drums dwindled. Night settled along Chang’an’s ward walls. In the chest containing Wang Meng’s papers, Yao Chang’s name remained unmarked in vermilion. On Fu Liang’s charred list, the final entry preserved only a surname; half a character had burned away. Beside it lay an empty line, as though waiting for an army that had not yet arrived.
Fu Jian lifted the sheet between finger and thumb. How thin it was. After those nights of rain and fire, half a realm's lives had been reduced to the weight of a page.
